title: Section 194 — Promoting enmity between different groups on grounds of religion, race, place of birth, residence, language, etc.

Introduction and meaning
Affray. BNS restatement of IPC 159 / 160. Elements are substantially the same; cite the BNS number for offences on or after 1 July 2024. BNS restatement of IPC 159 / 160. Cite the BNS number for facts on or after 1 July 2024.
In student language: BNS s. 194 is the rule on “Affray”. The section provides that (1) When two or more persons, by fighting in a public place, disturb the public peace, they are said to commit an affray. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 194 exists so that “Affray” has a closed legal test in Chapter XI — Of Offences Against the Public Tranquillity. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: Unlawful assembly, common object, rioting, affray, and promoting enmity.

The provision in detail
194. (1) When two or more persons, by fighting in a public place, disturb the public peace, they are said to commit an affray

(2) Whoever commits an affray, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one month, or with fine which may extend to one thousand rupees, or with both

hypotheticals.question: Whether BNS s. 194 (Affray) applies, and how structured written arguments should be framed.
hypotheticals.analysis:
Step 1 — Identify the provision. The correct current-law cite is BNS s. 194 (Affray), Chapter XI — Of Offences Against the Public Tranquillity.
Step 2 — State the legal test in your own words, then list the ingredients:
   (1) When two or more persons, by fighting in a public place, disturb the public peace, they are said to commit an affray
   (2) Whoever commits an affray, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one month, or with fine which may extend to one thousand rupees, or with both
Step 3 — Check limitations, provisos and the rest of the Chapter so you do not apply s. 194 in a vacuum.
Step 4 — Map each fact to an ingredient. Write “this fact proves ingredient (a)” or “this fact is missing, so the section is not made out”.
Step 5 — Conclude. If every essential ingredient is proved and no exception covers the case, BNS s. 194 applies. If any essential ingredient fails, say so and stop. Do not invent a different section to save the answer.

Comprehensive Written Submissions. Deepen the doctrinal synthesis with four foundational layers.

Layer 1 — Place the section in the Chapter. Unlawful assembly, common object, rioting, affray, and promoting enmity.. Show why this heading sits where it sits.

Layer 2 — Work a second, slightly harder hypothetical. Change one ingredient and show why the section then fails.

enhancement.legalPrinciple: Protects communal harmony and social peace by criminalizing hate speech and acts prejudicial to harmony between religious, racial, linguistic, or regional groups.
statutoryFramework: Chapter XI — Of Offences against the Public Tranquillity, BNS s. 194.
Statutory Title: Promoting enmity between different groups on grounds of religion, race, place of birth, residence, language, etc..

Core Legal Mandate: (1) When two or more persons, by fighting in a public place, disturb the public peace, they are said to commit an affray
(2) Whoever commits an affray, shall be punished with imprisonment of either de...
Classification and Sentencing: Structured under Chapter XI penal tiers.
Evidentiary and Procedural Cognate: Governed by the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 and Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023.
essentialIngredients: The commission of an act or omission falling within the statutory description of Promoting enmity between different groups on grounds of religion, race, place of birth, residence, language, etc..
The existence of the requisite culpable mental state (intention, knowledge, rashness, or negligence) prescribed under Section 194.
The absence of any statutory justification, exception, or lawful authority under Chapter III (General Exceptions).
The resulting consequence or endangerment specified in the statutory formula of Section 194.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 194 carries forward Section 153A IPC, targeting hate speech, communal incitement, and inter-group hostility. Sub-section (1) penalizes promoting enmity, hatred, or ill-will between different religious, racial, linguistic, or regional groups by words, signs, visible representations, or electronic communications, or doing acts prejudicial to harmony. Sub-section (2) establishes an aggravated tier—punishing such offences committed in places of worship or religious assemblies with imprisonment up to five years and fine. Mens rea requires deliberate intent to promote disharmony; fair academic debate or historical analysis without venom is protected.
examples: Teaching example (Standard application): An individual intentionally commits acts satisfying the statutory formula of promoting enmity between different groups on grounds of religion, race, place of birth, residence, language, etc. under Section 194 without lawful authority. The individual is liable under BNS s. 194.

Teaching example (Absence of mens rea / Lawful exception): A person acts in good faith or without the requisite statutory mental element under circumstances recognized by law. The essential ingredients of Section 194 are not satisfied; no penal liability attaches.
distinctions: Section 194 vs Section 299 (Outraging religious feelings): Section 194 focuses on inter-group enmity between different communities; Section 299 focuses on malicious insults directed at a religion itself.
Section 194 vs Section 195: Section 194 deals with enmity between groups; Section 195 deals with assertions prejudicial to national integration.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether the accused is liable under BNS s. 194 for conduct relating to promoting enmity between different groups on grounds of religion, race, place of birth, residence, language, etc..
Rule: Under BNS s. 194, liability attaches upon proof of the statutory actus reus accompanied by the requisite mens rea without lawful justification.
Application: The evidence demonstrates that the accused performed the specified act with the required state of mind, satisfying all statutory ingredients of Section 194.
Conclusion: The accused is guilty of an offence under BNS s. 194 and subject to the prescribed punishment.
